w: What's tested The major glands and their hormones, and the three hormone classes with an example of each ("you'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones") The oral findings of each disorder: acromegaly's growing jaw, hyper- and hypothyroidism, hyper- and hypoparathyroidism on the radiograph, Addison disease, Cushing syndrome, diabetes, and puberty, pregnancy and menopause His clinical points: implants wait until growth stops, the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery, epinephrine in hyperthyroidism, extra steroid after a big procedure in Addison disease The diabetic patient: his numbers (HbA1c above 7 is poorly controlled; a glucose under 60 needs sugar), the checks before treatment and the rescue for hypoglycemia: finger-stick, glucose rather than table sugar, glucagon if that fails Recognizing three emergencies: thyroid storm (call 911), adrenal crisis and hypoglycemia His three cases, which he walked through by asking the class: Graves disease, a type 2 diabetic who needs an extraction (and his pack-year question), and Addison disease with oral pigmentation 1 Hypoglycemia in the chair: the signs, a finger-stick (some CGMs stop reading at a floor), straight glucose rather than table sugar, a slow response on a GLP-1 drug, glucagon IM or subcutaneously if oral glucose fails Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this If a patient looks hypoglycemic, check a finger-stick even when the CGM shows a number: his patient's read 53 while she was in the 30s. Give straight glucose, not table sugar (half fructose); if oral glucose fails, IV dextrose or glucagon IM or subcutaneously, and expect a slow response on a GLP-1 drug. Two warnings from a patient of his. Some patients wear a continuous glucose monitor, or CGM, a sensor taped to the arm. Some CGMs only read down to a certain level: his patient's stopped at 53, and her finger-stick was in the 30s. It took 10 or 12 packets of glucose gel to bring her back. She also took Mounjaro, and GLP-1 drugs slow the gut, so glucose given by mouth reaches the blood more slowly than you expect. Not all sugars are the same. Table sugar, sucrose, is half glucose and half fructose, and the body can't use fructose (or galactose) directly: the liver has to convert it to glucose first. Straight glucose needs less processing, so it raises the blood sugar faster. 2 Before treating a diabetic: HbA1c above 7 is poorly controlled (implant failure, periodontal disease), confirm the meal and medication, morning appointments; Dr. Taylor's metformin with a skipped breakfast; pack-years Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this Above 7 percent is poor control (more implant failure and periodontal disease); below 7 is well controlled, and a person without diabetes runs about 5. Metformin inhibits gluconeogenesis, and he drew a chair-side warning from it. A type 2 diabetic took her medicines but skipped breakfast to make the appointment. She has blocked her own glucose production and eaten nothing, so in his example she is at high risk of hypoglycemia in your chair; be ready with glucose if she turns sweaty or agitated. (Lecture 11 teaches that metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia; insulin and the secretagogues are the usual cause. Either way, ask about the meal.) Finger-stick glucose under 60 Hypoglycemia: give sugar Fasting glucose well over 100 May have diabetes: insulin isn't clearing the blood HbA1c about 5 percent Typical for a person without diabetes HbA1c below 7 (below 6 even better) Generally well controlled HbA1c above 7 Poorly controlled: much higher risk of implant failure and of periodontal disease; plan treatment accordingly 3 Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease (his first case): epinephrine caution, and thyroid storm (fever, pulse 140 or more; call 911) Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Thyroid storm: high fever, a pulse of 140 or more, agitation and delirium in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism; call 911. Thyroid storm, also called thyroid crisis or thyrotoxic crisis, is rare, but it happens: the gland releases a large amount of hormone in a short time. It is a life-threatening emergency. The signs are a high fever, a rapid heart rate, 140 or higher, agitation, anxiety, shakiness, nausea and even delirium. "If you start to see signs and symptoms of this, call 911." In his Graves case, the first thing he would check is the heart rate. 4 Addison disease (his third case): oral pigment from high ACTH, adrenal crisis triggers and signs, extra corticosteroid after a big procedure; Cushing syndrome and long-term steroids Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this An Addison patient can't raise cortisol for surgical stress: know the crisis triggers (long surgery, infection or trauma, a missed dose) and plan extra steroid with the physician. Adrenal crisis is the emergency of Addison disease. It can be set off by stressful or lengthy surgical procedures, significant infection or trauma, and a missed steroid dose. Any stressful event, an extraction included, normally makes the body produce more corticosteroid, and these patients can't, so after a bigger procedure they may need supplemental corticosteroid, usually a larger dose than normal; agree on the dose with their physician first. The signs of a crisis are severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness and shock. Cortisol Too little (often with low aldosterone) Too much (or long-term steroid therapy) Clinical features Hypotension, fatigue, hyperpigmentation Moon face, buffalo hump, hyperglycemia In the mouth Brown patches; diffuse oral melanosis Increased infection risk, delayed healing Emergency Adrenal crisis; extra steroid after a big procedure None listed 5 Hyperparathyroidism on the radiograph (lost lamina dura, radiolucent brown tumors, mobility) and the calcium regulators (PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin) Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Vitamin D is the long-term regulator. We make it in the skin in an inactive form; the active form comes from the kidney, and it helps the gut absorb calcium. You may also see brown tumors and tooth mobility. A brown tumor shows on a panoramic radiograph as a radiolucent area; his example sat in the bone below a premolar. If you find one, ask the patient about other symptoms and send them to their physician to be checked. 6 Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Acromegaly in an adult shows the dentist a growing mandible: a bite moving from Class I to edge-to-edge or Class III, new diastemas and a large tongue. The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates; plan a young patient's implant for after growth stops. Growth hormone stays with you for life, but it is strongest in childhood and adolescence. What stops the long bones from growing is the sex hormones: at puberty the growth plates fuse, and growth hormone no longer lengthens them. He uses this in treatment planning. A 13- or 14-year-old boy who is growing hair on his upper lip is probably close to puberty and near his final height. If a patient lost a tooth at 10, he waits for growth to stop before placing an implant: an implant is fixed in the bone, and if the face is still growing, everything moves around it. Too much growth hormone before puberty, while the long bones are still open, makes a person very tall, 7 feet or more. After puberty the long bones are fused, so they barely grow, and the condition is acromegaly. The hands and feet enlarge, but "look for the jaw in your patients": the mandible grows, so the bite changes, from a normal Class I to edge-to-edge or even a Class III malocclusion. The bigger arch leaves more room for the teeth, so diastemas open between them, and the tongue enlarges (macroglossia). Macroglossia also appears under hypothyroidism, so it is the jaw and the spacing that point to growth hormone. 7 The three hormone classes with examples, receptors, and endocrine versus nervous signaling Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank He contrasted it with the nervous system, which does similar work in a different way. Speed of response: the nervous system is always faster, because it works on electrical signals through nerves spread all over the body. The endocrine system releases its hormones into the bloodstream, and the blood takes time to carry them around. Duration of action: hormones act longer, and they also take longer to shut off, so when the endocrine system overreacts, the body takes longer to bring it back under control. 8 Diabetes: type 1 versus type 2 (insulin ineffective, not deficient), oral manifestations and the sugar in saliva, the two-way periodontal link, SGLT2 drugs and UTIs Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank The oral manifestations of diabetes are xerostomia (the most common, but not specific), candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, and an increased risk of periodontal disease and of dental caries. Why the candidiasis and caries: saliva is filtered blood, so a high blood glucose puts more sugar in the saliva, which feeds Candida and Streptococcus mutans. 9 Hyperthyroid versus hypothyroid dental considerations (hypothyroidism far more common), and the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Thyroid and parathyroid surgery puts the recurrent laryngeal nerve at risk: damage leaves a hoarse, raspy voice, usually for good. A surgical point he made from his years in the operating room: the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs through the thyroid area, and the first thing a surgeon does in a thyroidectomy or a parathyroidectomy is find it. Damage to it paralyzes half of the vocal cords, leaving a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent. 10 Sex hormones and the mouth: puberty, pregnancy gingivitis and the interproximal pyogenic granuloma, menopause Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Puberty Increased gingival inflammation Pregnancy Pregnancy gingivitis; pyogenic granuloma, the "pregnancy tumor", usually interproximal Menopause Xerostomia; altered taste; osteoporosis implications 11 Pituitary hormones (ADH and diabetes insipidus), alpha and beta cells, and the adrenal medulla Objectives · 3 questions in the bank The posterior pituitary has two hormones. ADH conserves water. Too little ADH is diabetes insipidus: the kidneys let out far too much fluid, so the patient is very thirsty all the time. Don't confuse it with diabetes mellitus, the insulin disease: same first word, different hormone. Oxytocin, the "connection hormone" of delivery, is the other. His trivia: alcohol lowers ADH (so you urinate) and nicotine raises it. Also flagged in class Know the three classes with an example of each, and that steroids act on receptors inside the cell while peptides bind on the surface. Expect hypothyroid patients (fatigue, weight gain, macroglossia, slow healing, usually on thyroid hormone) far more often than hyperthyroid ones. Know what PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin each do, and read hyperparathyroidism on a radiograph: lost lamina dura, radiolucent brown tumors, loose teeth. He said he hadn't given the class this one, so he told them: in Addison disease low cortisol lets ACTH rise, and ACTH darkens the skin and oral mucosa. Pack-years = packs per day times years smoked: one pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years. In type 2 diabetes insulin is ineffective, not deficient; autoimmune beta-cell destruction is type 1. You can skip His aside that alcohol lowers ADH and nicotine raises it was offered as trivia; know ADH's job and diabetes insipidus instead.
